source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Founding paradigm (from the 1980 study, as described in the 1983 intro). Subjects read a military story (General/fortress, convergence solution), then solve Duncker's radiation problem. With an explicit hint to use the story, most produce the convergence solution. Controls with no story rarely do.
numbers: About 75% convergence with story plus hint; under 10% in controls with no story; about 30% when the story was memorised and no hint was given. Base rate 10% assumed from several replications.
quote: about 75% of those subjects who received the appropriate military analog produced the convergence solution
limits: 1980 figures are second-hand here (the 1980 PDF was not available). Radiation problem is ill-defined, so an analogy can steer the solution. College students only.
agent_relevance: Having an analogue in context is not enough. Noticing is the weak step; application is easy once noticed. O7 needs an explicit step that checks stored analogues against the current problem.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Noticing vs applying gap: only a third or less of subjects who could use the analogy noticed it spontaneously. A hint raised success from about 30% to about 75%.
numbers: 30% no hint vs 75% with hint; with 10% base rate, (30-10)/(75-10) is about 31% of potential appliers noticed it spontaneously.
limits: Estimate relies on the assumed 10% base rate.
agent_relevance: Retrieval, not mapping, is the bottleneck. A scaffold step that forces 'what known problem has this structure?' targets the real failure.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 1 (Part I), cord problem (Maier two-string). An analogous story gives the pendulum solution much more often than a control story. Recall vs summary instructions do not differ.
numbers: Before hint: analog groups combined 71% vs control 20% (G2(1)=15.8, p<.001). Total: 98% vs 30% (G2(1)=30.1, p<.001). N=69: 25 analog-recall, 24 analog-summary, 20 control.
limits: Different problem from radiation, so the effect is not specific to one problem. Table text has OCR noise in the source copy.
agent_relevance: A matching story strongly boosts solution of a second, different problem type.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 2 (Part I): stating the abstract principle in words did not help one-analog transfer. Analog plus principle equals analog only.
numbers: Convergence before hint: analog+principle 32% (10 of 31), analog only 29% (8 of 28), principle only 28% (8 of 29). Total 80%, 79%, 66%. N=88. Group difference not significant (total G2(2)=2.05, p=.36).
limits: Principle alone was already about as good as analog alone, so the design cannot separate the two cleanly.
agent_relevance: A one-line rule in the prompt does not replace a worked second case.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 3 (Part I): a diagram of the convergence idea paired with one story did not help noticing. Diagram-only subjects almost never found the solution unprompted but could after a hint.
numbers: Combined analog conditions 31% before hint; diagram-only 1 of 15 (7%) before hint, 67% total (vs 78% for analog conditions). N=66.
limits: Only one diagram form tried.
agent_relevance: Visual aids alone do not trigger retrieval either.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 4 (Part II): two analogs plus a request to describe their similarities led many subjects to write a general schema, and schema quality strongly predicted transfer.
numbers: N=98 (28 two-similar, 23 two-dissimilar, 47 analog+control). Two-analog groups 45% before hint vs one-analog 21%; total 80% vs 53% (G2(1)=8.36, p<.003). Good schema: 91% (10 of 11) solved before hint and 100% total; poor schema: 30% before hint, 70% total (30 subjects scored in the schema table). Overall 21% good, 20% intermediate, 59% poor schemas.
limits: Correlational: skilled solvers may both write good schemas and transfer well. Good schemas were rare.
agent_relevance: Comparing two cases to extract the shared structure is the strongest known lever. O7 should compare at least two analogues and write the common schema, not map a single source.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 5: adding an explicit statement of the principle to two analogs raised noticing. The principle that failed alone with one story helped with two.
numbers: With principle: 62% before hint, 82% total; without: 40% before hint, 67% total (G2(1)=6.75 p<.01; G2(1)=4.34 p<.05). N=143. Good schemas 44% (with principle) vs 10%; poor 23% vs 60%.
limits: Schema scoring was by the authors.
agent_relevance: Write the schema, then apply it. Principle plus two cases beats either alone.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 6: diagrams plus two analogs gave the highest transfer rate in the series.
numbers: Diagram vs no diagram: 57% vs 37% before hint (G2(1)=7.55 p<.01); 92% vs 79% total (G2(1)=6.66 p<.01). N=189. Good schemas 55% (diagram) vs 28% (none). A further diagram condition: 68% before hint and 95% total (N=37).
limits: Similar vs dissimilar analog pairs: good schemas 65% vs 44% in favour of similar pairs.
agent_relevance: A diagram works after two cases exist, not before. A structure-rendering step helps after comparison.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer
finding: Exp 1: spontaneous analogical transfer can be large when the source is a textbook problem read days earlier. Source was a lightbulb/laser problem; targets were the lightbulb problem and the radiation problem.
numbers: Analogy group (N=21): 81% convergence on the lightbulb target and 86% on radiation; control (N=10): 10% and 10%. G2(1)=15.2, p<.001 for lightbulb. 4 of 21 failed.
limits: Source and target share some surface (rays, instruments); delay of days, but source learned in class.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous transfer is not hopeless. It depends on how similar the source looks to the target.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer
finding: Exp 2 factorial: surface similarity (laser vs ultrasound) and structural similarity (fragile glass vs insufficient intensity) both reduce spontaneous retrieval about equally. They do not interact.
numbers: Convergence before hint: laser+fragile glass 69%, ultrasound+fragile 38%, laser+insufficient 33%, ultrasound+insufficient 13%. Row means: fragile 54 vs insufficient 23; column means: laser 51 vs ultrasound 26. Reported noticing: 88, 56, 40, 13%.
limits: Surface effect G2(1)=4.42, p<.05; structure G2(1)=5.92, p<.05. Total N not read from the passages opened.
agent_relevance: Both surface cues and causal-structure cues feed retrieval. Restate the problem in terms that share both.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer
finding: After a hint, surface similarity no longer mattered but structural similarity still did. Surface cues affect retrieval; structure affects both retrieval and mapping.
numbers: Total (with hint): fragile glass 78% vs insufficient 54% (G2(1)=4.31, p<.05); laser 68% vs ultrasound 64% (G2(1)<1). Logit model: surface effect differed between before-hint and total (Wald=4.20, p<.05); structure effect did not (Wald=1.58, p>.20).
limits: Summaries of the insufficient-intensity story mentioned using different directions less often (30% vs 66%), so structural dissimilarity reduced encoding of the key idea.
agent_relevance: Support for the systematicity claim in problem solving: once the analogue is in hand, mapping quality tracks causal structure, not surface look.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer
finding: Proposed a retrieval mechanism: summation of activation from features shared by source and target, both causal and surface. Four-step account of analogy use: represent, select source, map, extend mapping to a solution.
numbers: Four steps named: (1) represent source and target, (2) select source, (3) map components, (4) extend mapping to a solution.
limits: Verbal model in this paper; computational versions are ACME and ARCS.
agent_relevance: Matches a two-part design for O7: cheap retrieval over many cases, then a structural check.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Exp 1: explicit comparison of two analogs gives pre-hint transfer under minimal delay and the same context.
numbers: Two analogs, compare: 47% before hint, 68% total (n=19); one analog plus control, compare: 16% before hint, 53% total (n=19). Two-analog groups combined total 71% vs 41% for one-analog (G2(1)=7.16, p<.01).
limits: No no-analog control group; 10% baseline taken from earlier work. Same session, same room.
agent_relevance: Replicates Gick & Holyoak 1983. Comparison pays off before a hint only with two analogs.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Exp 2-3: boundary condition. Spontaneous transfer collapses after a context shift or delay when the analogs are dissimilar from the target; hints still work.
numbers: Exp 2: no condition exceeded the 10% pre-hint baseline; total 65% (30-min delay) vs 42% (1-week delay) (G2(1)=4.64, p<.05). Pre-hint at one week: 7% (Exp 2) and 23% (Exp 3). Exp 2 one-week subjects with appropriate schemas: 40% vs 6% pre-hint for inappropriate (G2(1)=6.19, p<.02, as read from the Exp 3 text).
limits: Hints worked, so the relevant features were still in memory. The failure is retrieval cueing.
agent_relevance: Memory is not the problem; cueing is. A scaffold must create cues at the target, not just store analogues.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Exp 4-5: transfer was recovered after a context shift and a one-week delay by three changes together: reword the target to stress the shared structure (intensity wording), give three analogs, and use detailed schema-oriented comparison questions.
numbers: Exp 4: directive comparison 36% vs 10% pre-hint, 70% vs 42% total (G2(1)=5.52, p<.02); intensity wording 32% vs dosage wording 14% pre-hint. Exp 5 (one-week delay): 74% overall produced the convergence solution before the hint (vs 7% and 23% in Exp 2 and 3). Appropriate schema 81% vs poor schema 0% pre-hint (only 2 subjects had poor schemas).
limits: Three manipulations are confounded in Exp 5. The reworded target shares a word with the sources.
agent_relevance: Restating the current problem in the schema's vocabulary is a cheap retrieval cue. Candidate operator step: rename target elements into schema terms before search.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: ACME: a localist constraint-satisfaction network for analogical mapping. One unit per possible element pairing; excitatory links enforce structural consistency, inhibitory links enforce one-to-one; semantic similarity and pragmatic importance add bias.
numbers: Three constraints: structural (isomorphism), semantic similarity, pragmatic centrality. Activation updates until the network settles; 'cycles to success' is used as a difficulty measure.
limits: Needs a unit for every possible pairing, which scales badly. Constraints are soft, not absolute.
agent_relevance: Isomorphism is treated as pressure, not a requirement: partial maps are accepted. A coded map-checker should score one-to-one and consistency rather than demand exact match.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: ACME simulated the Holyoak & Koh lightbulb/radiation convergence analogies. It finds the right mapping for all four versions; the two poor-constraint versions are slower and leave a key proposition unmapped.
numbers: In the poor-constraint versions the radiation proposition about not destroying healthy tissue (d22) has no map at all. ACME also mapped radiation to the fortress story. Exact cycle counts are not recorded (OCR of Table 5 garbled).
limits: Table 5 in the source copy is badly OCR'd. ACME models mapping only; the human percentages (69/38/33/13) are before-hint retrieval data. With a hint, humans mapped laser and ultrasound versions equally well, as ACME did.
agent_relevance: A target constraint with no counterpart in the source predicts failed transfer. Check that every goal constraint in the target has a counterpart.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: ACME is framed as the structural/semantic/pragmatic account and contrasted with SME (Gentner). ACME treats isomorphism softly and lets meaning similarity and purpose steer the map; SME builds from identical predicates and favours systematicity.
numbers: Section comparing with SME: both use higher-order relations to constrain mapping; ACME can map across different predicates when semantic similarity supports it.
limits: Comparison written by ACME's authors.
agent_relevance: Goal relevance should weight which correspondences matter. Pragmatic centrality is a useful input to O7.

source: Thagard, Holyoak, Nelson & Gochfeld (1990) Analog retrieval by constraint satisfaction (ARCS)
finding: ARCS: retrieval as constraint satisfaction. A probe is compared to a memory of structures; units for plausible pairings compete; semantic similarity (WordNet-style hierarchies), structure and goal relevance all feed activation.
numbers: Databases: 5 radiation problems, 5 Karla-the-hawk stories, 100 fables, 25 play synopses. Networks typically settle in under 150 cycles. Largest Karla simulation: 570 units, 26,330 links, did not settle in 200 cycles. Max 587 units in fable runs.
limits: Hand-coded predicate calculus. Cost grows with memory size.
agent_relevance: Use a cheap pre-filter then a structural check; do not run the full match over all of memory.

source: Thagard, Holyoak, Nelson & Gochfeld (1990) Analog retrieval by constraint satisfaction (ARCS)
finding: ARCS reproduced the ordering of human retrieval of radiation analogs: four lightbulb versions and the fortress problem.
numbers: Human no-hint solution rates (Holyoak & Koh 1987): laser/fragile 69%, ultrasound/fragile 38%, laser/insufficient 33%, ultrasound/insufficient 13%; fortress about 30% (approximate average over Gick & Holyoak). ARCS asymptotic activation for laser/fragile 0.22; others lower (OCR rows scrambled).
limits: Fit is by rank order, not a quantitative statistic.
agent_relevance: Computational support that a weighted sum of semantic, structural and goal cues predicts which analog comes to mind.

source: Thagard, Holyoak, Nelson & Gochfeld (1990) Analog retrieval by constraint satisfaction (ARCS)
finding: ARCS also modelled Karla-the-hawk retrieval with 100 fables as distractors. The order literal similarity > mere appearance > true analogy > false analogy was reproduced with one small reversal.
numbers: Human rates (inferred from a graph by the ARCS authors): literal similarity 58%, mere appearance 45%, true analogy 18%, false analogy 8%. Karla unit ranked 1 of 68 for literal similarity.
limits: Human percentages were read off a graph; differences in human data fell short of significance but replicated in two experiments.
agent_relevance: True analogues are retrieved far less often than look-alikes; do not rely on unaided recall of the deep match.

source: Gentner & Forbus (1991) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: Karla-the-hawk memory study: people retrieve surface matches more readily than true analogies from long-term memory, yet rate analogies as more sound. Retrieval and judged soundness dissociate.
numbers: Remindings from a 32-story memory set (20 base, 12 distractor) after two weeks: literal similarity .56, surface (SF) .53, analogy .12, first-order-only (FOR) .09. Order LS > SF > AN > FOR stable across three variations.
limits: Short invented stories; college students. Higher-order relations helped retrieval only slightly (non-significant in two studies, small in a third).
agent_relevance: Core boundary condition: the best analogue is the one least likely to be retrieved. Retrieval must be engineered, not trusted.

source: Gentner & Forbus (1991) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval
finding: MAC/FAC: two stages. MAC is a cheap content-vector dot-product filter. FAC runs a structure-mapping match on the survivors. Output is the best match plus anything within 10%.
numbers: Sim 1 (9 base plus 9 FOR in memory): correct retrieval LS 1.0/1.0, SF .89/.89, AN .67 (MAC) and .56 (FAC). Sim 2 (36 stories): MAC returns 3.3 items on average, FAC accepts 1.5. Sim 3 (LS removed): SF is the clear winner.
limits: Memory sets of 18 to 36 stories are far smaller than human memory; the model beats humans, which authors attribute to smaller memory and shorter delay.
agent_relevance: Direct pattern for O7: cheap broad retrieval, then expensive structural check on a few candidates. It also predicts surface false friends will be retrieved, so the check must reject them.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Qualitative test of the Gick & Holyoak radiation paradigm on GPT-3 (text-davinci-003). In isolation GPT-3 proposed a non-convergent solution (place the source inside the tumor). After reading the general story it gave the convergence solution and listed the mappings.
numbers: Single-item demonstrations, no counts. Mappings: general to doctor, dictator to tumor, army to rays. Same result with a lightbulb/laser source story.
limits: Qualitative only, no repeated sampling; source story adjacent to target (no retrieval needed).
agent_relevance: A model can apply a supplied analogue. This says nothing about retrieving one.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: With two distractor stories added, GPT-3 lost the convergence solution and reverted to the non-analogical answer. When told to consider the previous stories, it picked the general story as most relevant and produced the convergence solution.
numbers: One run each (Supplementary S5.4, S5.5).
limits: Qualitative; sample of one. In-context only: once the context was cleared the model reverted.
agent_relevance: Same failure and same hint fix as humans: a forced 'which earlier case fits?' step is the hint.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogy test with Gentner et al. materials: GPT-3 prefers the target that shares causal (higher-order) relations in near analogies but not significantly in far (cross-domain) ones. Humans (N=54) managed both.
numbers: GPT-3 combined binomial p=.0005; near p=.0039; far p=.065 (ns). Humans t(53)=21.3 combined, 21.5 near, 16.7 far. Humans beat GPT-3: OR=0.37, p=.0003; 15 of 54 humans chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-4 initial check: near-perfect on near, more robust on far.
limits: GPT-3 only for main numbers; GPT-4 shown in a supplement.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain causal mapping is the weakest link in models, the exact condition systematicity theory is about.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Gumball/genie transfer task (children's paradigm of Holyoak, Junn & Billman): GPT-3 named all major correspondences between the genie story and the bowl task but could not use them to find a workable physical solution.
numbers: Qualitative. Solutions were 'elaborate, but mechanically nonsensical'. The authors blame missing physical reasoning, not mapping.
limits: Text only, no real objects, unlike the children's task.
agent_relevance: Mapping and solution feasibility are separate. Add a code or simulation check on the mapped plan.

source: Puranam, Sen & Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? Humans and GPT-4
finding: Gick-and-Holyoak-style matching task with two source stories and two targets (Radiation, Dolphin). Humans (n=199) were conservative: high precision, low recall. GPT-4 (n=60 runs) with no hint never claimed the correct source. With a hint it always did, but over-applied.
numbers: No hint: AI TP 0 of 15 for both cases (precision 0, recall 0, accuracy .50); humans radiation TP 3, FN 45, FP 4, TN 55 (precision .42, recall .06); dolphin TP 13, FN 46, FP 0 (precision 1.0, recall .22). With hint: AI recall 1.00, precision .52 and .50 (F1 .68, .67); humans precision .67 and .75, recall .26 and .39.
limits: The abstract says GPT-4 had high recall; that holds in the hint condition only. Hint wording may invite over-claiming (authors cite demand effects). Business-school students; one model; some OCR noise in the tables.
agent_relevance: LLM profile is the mirror of the human one: no spontaneous retrieval, then indiscriminate matching once prompted. A code-run check is needed to cut false positives.

source: Puranam, Sen & Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? Humans and GPT-4
finding: Error patterns: GPT-4 misapplied analogies from surface similarity; human errors were subtler misreadings of causal logic.
numbers: Counts as in the confusion matrices of the previous line.
limits: Single model; error coding by the authors.
agent_relevance: Add a mapping-consistency check, not just a similarity score.

source: Barakat & Kochmar (2026) Teaching through analogies: a modular pipeline for educational analogy generation
finding: Pipeline grounded in structure-mapping: find source, generate sub-concept pairings, explain, judge. Sub-concepts (aligned parts) raise closed-set retrieval precision and explanation quality but add little to open-ended source generation. Cites earlier results: LLMs distracted by surface similarity (30% vs 85% human) and system accuracy 62% (GPT-4) vs 86% (humans).
numbers: Closed-set Hit@1: gold sub-concepts 24.5%, background 22.2%, gold+background 20.8%, embedding only 19.5%, generated sub-concepts 18.2%, names only 17.5%. Open-setting gains only 0.4 to 1.6 points. Best Hit@20 about 75.4% (Gemini-2.5). 12 LLMs, 7 embedding models, 7 human annotators, 45 analogy pairs.
limits: Educational analogies, not problem solving. The 30% vs 85% and 62% vs 86% figures are cited from other papers, not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Listing the parts of the target before searching helps closed-set retrieval. For open generation extra structure gave almost nothing, so keep the step cheap.

source: Gentner & Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy
finding: Systematicity aids mapping, but only once children are about 8. Children (N=72; 36 aged 4-6, 36 aged 8-10) acted out a target story from a source story, with systematic (causal-moral) or nonsystematic versions and three object-correspondence conditions.
numbers: Age F(1,68)=14.93 p<.001; Systematicity F(1,68)=6.28 p<.05; Mapping condition F(2,136)=29.01 p<.000001; Systematicity x Mapping F(2,136)=3.89 p<.05. Older children better on systematic stories t(34)=2.48 p<.01; younger no benefit t(34)=1.08 ns.
limits: Children's story-acting task, not a problem-solving task. Younger children showed no systematicity advantage.
agent_relevance: Systematic structure helps when object matches are misleading (cross-mapped), the case O7 must handle.

source: Gentner & Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy
finding: Systematicity acts at mapping, not memory: all children nearly perfect on the easy transfer, so differences are not forgetting. Older children self-corrected using the causal chain.
numbers: High-transparency mapping near perfect in both systematic and nonsystematic conditions; effect largest on the hardest (cross-mapped) condition.
limits: Self-corrections reported informally.
agent_relevance: Causal chains let a mapper repair a wrong local match. Use causal links to verify the mapping.
